title: Impossibility of superluminal signalling rules out causal loops in conical spacetimes
abstract: In PRL 129, 110401 it was shown that it is theoretically possible to have operationally detectable causal loops without violating the principle of no superluminal signalling (NSS) in (1+1)-Minkowski spacetime. Whether or not such causal loops are also possible in $d > 1$ spatial dimensions, has remained a key open question. We resolve this question by showing that in a wide class of "conical" spacetimes, including Minkowski with d > 1, NSS does rule out all operationally detectable causal loops, in classical, quantum and post-quantum theories. This establishes that the relationship between the relativistic principles of NSS and no causal loops depends inherently on the geometry of spacetime.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates the relationship between superluminal signaling constraints (NSS) and causal loops in spacetime. By introducing the concept of 'conicality,' the authors prove that this geometric property forces any compatible causal structure to be non-looping, thereby establishing a deep link between local causality principles and global spacetime geometry.
main_problem: The central problem is determining whether the principle of No Superluminal Signalling (NSS) inherently rules out all operationally detectable causal loops in spacetimes that possess a 'conical' geometric structure.
main_result: The authors prove a general no-go result: in any conical spacetime, NSS rules out all operationally verifiable causal loops, establishing that this relationship depends fundamentally on the geometry of spacetime.
method: The analysis uses an advanced framework combining causal inference (affects relations) with geometric constraints derived from poset theory, specifically leveraging the concept of 'conicality' in the spacetime embedding.
model_or_system: The model involves describing causality using directed graphs and affects relations, which are then embedded into a partially ordered set (poset) representing the spacetime light cone structure. The focus is on 'conical' spacetimes, including $d>1$ Minkowski space.
key_observables: Operationally detectable causal loops (ACLs), compatibility conditions derived from affects relations ($	ext{X} \models 	ext{Y} | 	ext{do}(	ext{Z})$), and the geometric property of conicality.
important_parameters: The spatial dimension $d$ (comparing $d=1$ vs. $d>1$), and the irreducibility conditions ($	ext{Irred1}, 	ext{Irred3}$) applied to affects relations.
main_assumptions: The entire proof structure relies heavily on assuming a conical embedding of the causal model into spacetime, as this geometric property is key to deriving contradictions that rule out loops.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates complex examples of ACLs in $(1+1)$-Minkowski space. Figure 2 compares light cone representations for $d=1$ (non-conical) versus $d>1$ (conical), showing how joint futures differ.
paper_structure: The paper develops the framework by first defining affects relations and conical embeddings, then proving necessary lemmas that simplify higher-order conditional affects relations ($	ext{Lemma A.7}$). Finally, it applies these results to prove that any compatible embedding of ACLs in a conical spacetime must be degenerate (Theorem A.9).
why_interesting: While not directly related to quantum many-body physics, the rigorous mathematical framework for causality and information flow across curved spacetimes is foundational for theories involving quantum gravity or relativistic quantum field theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Let X, Y, Z, A, B ∈S. Consider X ⊨Y, Y ⊨AB, A ⊨X, Z ⊨AB, B ⊨Z. (a) No matter the underlying causal model, the affects relations allow to infer that a causal loop will always be present. Here, ↠denotes causal relations between two RVs, while its dashed version stands for alternative causal relations, e.g. Y ↠AB being equivalent to (Y ↠A or Y ↠B), so at least one of the dashed arrows from Y must be present as a causal relation. (b) A compatible, non-degenerate embedding of these affects relations into (1 + 1)-Minkowski spacetime, where all ORVs need be located on certain light-like surfaces.

Figure 2: Representation of light cones in Minkowski spacetime for d spatial dimensions. (a) For d = 1 Minkowski spacetime does not show conicality. This is because L1 := {a, b} and L2 := {x, y} are distinct, yet share the same joint future. (b) For d = 2, Minkowski spacetime is conical. As can be seen from the figure which shows one particular time slice, the joint futures are distinct between L1 and L2 (and the red region is thus not covered by the blue one).
